headline: Oxevision, an AI-powered camera system used in NHS mental health hospitals, is under scrutiny over consent and privacy, and its maker has acknowledged limits in its evidence to a public inquiry.
score_reason: Pool score kept: a vulnerable group, a system in about half of England's mental health trusts and a public inquiry, though the report gives concerns and a company response rather than findings.
importance_line: Patients detained in mental health wards, and their families, may be filmed in their bedrooms without clear consent, while the maker says the system helps protect them, and the inquiry has yet to decide what to recommend.
summary: Channel 4 News reports that Oxevision, a system whose cameras track patients' pulse and breathing in their bedrooms and which is used in about half of the mental health trusts (local organisations) of England's National Health Service (NHS), is being examined at the Lampard Inquiry into mental health patient deaths in Essex, where families and former patients have raised concerns about privacy, consent and whether cameras are replacing human care. The maker, LIO Health, told Channel 4 the system was never designed to replace nurses and that it does not tell organisations how to use it, and it has acknowledged limitations in its evidence to the inquiry.
notes: The channel4.com page in the pool is a short video blurb; the full written version of the same Ayshah Tull report was read at channel4news.substack.com/p/why-cameras-in-mental-health-bedrooms. The BBC (6 Oct 2026) reported the inquiry hearing in which NHS England said 10 trusts were not running consent processes in line with its digital principles; that is context only and not in the summary.
